title: Houthis Threaten Bab el-Mandeb as Gulf Oil Recovers and Washington Trades Sanctions for Barrels
subhead: A Houthi missile and drone strike on Saudi Arabia's Sharurah base and a push toward Mocha put the Red Sea exit in play just as Gulf crude flows recover to about 80% of pre-war levels. Meanwhile Trump waives the Graham Act, Baghdad weighs an $8bn farm diesel package, and a Qatari LNG cargo takes the Suez run for the first time in months.

sections.heading: The Red Sea exit becomes the second front
sections.body:
Yemen's Houthis claimed a ballistic missile and drone attack on Saudi Arabia's Sharurah base in the south of the kingdom, with military spokesman Yahya Saree saying the strikes hit weapons depots and command centres and warning of larger attacks deeper inside Saudi territory if operations in Yemen continue, according to Middle East Eye. The attack came as clashes with Riyadh-backed government forces intensified around Mocha, and as Houthi forces made territorial gains along Yemen's western coast.

The timing is what matters. Saudi Arabia's main East-West pipeline — roughly 1,200 km of crude moving from the eastern fields to Red Sea terminals, the only serious bypass of Hormuz — was shut in September after drone attacks launched from Iraq's Maysan province, with Iraqi authorities tracing the launch site to the al-Tayeb border district near the Sheeb crossing, Middle East Eye and Al Jazeera reported. Repairs have kept it mostly out of service.

With Hormuz still disrupted, the Red Sea corridor is now the last working exit for Saudi barrels — and it terminates at Bab el-Mandeb, exactly where the Houthis are closing in.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia has no third route. If the Houthis gain the ability to threaten Red Sea loadings from Mocha or the islands off the coast, the kingdom's export capacity shrinks to whatever Hormuz will allow — and that is still below normal.

sections.heading: Brent touches $109.99, then fades on demand fears
sections.body:
Brent crude briefly hit $109.99 a barrel overnight — a five-month high — before retreating, with Asian media quoting Brent futures at $109.76 and ZeroHedge putting the pullback at 3.5% to the $103 handle by early US hours after an IEA warning that fuel costs could trigger demand destruction. Prices are up more than 70% this year.

RBC's Helima Croft flagged a full Saudi-Houthi war as the catalyst for the bank's high-price scenario. UBS's Justinus Steinhorst noted Brent holding above $105 with Bab el-Mandeb disruption creating a double-chokepoint fear, alongside 10-year Bund yields at their highest since 2009. Sparta Commodities analyst June Goh told Bloomberg the market is unwilling to absorb higher prices with the broader economy weak, and expects Brent to hold near $100.

The offset: Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Gulf oil flows have recovered to roughly 80% of pre-conflict levels, and told ABC News that gasoline and diesel prices 'peaked a few weeks ago.'
sections.whyItMatters: The market is now pricing two contradictory things at once — recovering crude supply and an unresolved product crisis. That is why crude swung $7 in a session while diesel barely moved.

sections.heading: Diesel is still the real crisis — and Washington is paying for it
sections.body:
The IEA reports global diesel and gasoil availability running 1.7 million b/d below year-earlier levels in Q3 2026, after a 1.5 million b/d gap in Q2, according to analysis citing the agency's data. The US motor fuels index rose 60.9% year on year in September. AAA pump data put diesel at $6.319 a gallon on Sunday against a record $6.50, and gasoline at $4.295 — still above the politically sensitive $4 mark.

The IEA expects the squeeze to last well into 2027. Wright told Fox News that Washington is discussing coordinated diesel stockpile releases with European allies. Trump also said the USDA will launch what he called a $8 billion 'harvest fuel relief' programme for farmers to offset diesel costs, Reuters reported from Kansas.

The structural reason diesel is worse than crude: it needs specific refinery units, tight sulphur specs and dedicated storage. Middle distillates are nearly 30% of global oil demand, so refinery damage — Middle East strikes plus Ukraine's campaign against Russian plants — hits a huge share of the market at once.
sections.whyItMatters: Crude can be rerouted; diesel cannot. Subsidy programmes and stockpile releases treat the symptom. Until refining capacity returns, diesel keeps feeding inflation into food, freight and manufacturing.

sections.heading: Trump trades sanctions for barrels, and Europe splits
sections.body:
Trump defended his October 16 executive order waiving sanctions mandated by the Graham Act, writing on Truth Social that he is 'in the process of negotiating Peace' and does not want to 'drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.' He had already granted temporary relief on Russian diesel sanctions. Rubio publicly framed the waiver as a 60-day review, but the executive order sets no end date, per reporting on the text.

Zelenskyy told NBC's Meet the Press that 'if the United States will take the side of Russia, of course we will not prevail,' and said intelligence-sharing that had been interrupted now appears 'de-blocked.' Trump responded by questioning whether Zelenskyy should be at the table at all, saying 'maybe it's time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate,' and told reporters he is open to talks with Putin and Xi Jinping — potentially without Kyiv.

In Europe, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev broke ranks at the EU summit, saying 'you know what is our problem right now in Europe? High fuel prices,' and criticising Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries: 'I don't support strikes on any refineries.' Brussels condemned the diesel deal as a concession to Putin; EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas sided with Kyiv.
sections.whyItMatters: The waiver has no sunset and no conditions attached to Russian behaviour. That converts a sanctions regime into a price-management tool — and gives Moscow a revenue floor while it strikes Ukrainian power plants ahead of winter.

sections.heading: A Qatari LNG cargo takes the Suez route — a signal, not a recovery
sections.body:
A Qatari LNG cargo is moving north through the Red Sea toward Poland via the Suez Canal, Bloomberg vessel-tracking data showed — a rare shipment on the shortest but most dangerous route to Europe. The cargo loaded in August. QatarEnergy holds a term contract with Polish group Orlen.

The broader picture is grim: since the Iran war began, Hormuz closed and attacks damaged Qatar's Ras Laffan complex, the world's largest single LNG liquefaction site. QatarEnergy has extended its force majeure every month since first declaring it in early March. Most LNG carriers now transit Hormuz in dark mode, making flow estimates harder. Qatari LNG exports are nowhere near the pace of recovery seen in Middle East crude exports.

Qatar's Deputy PM and Defence Minister Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani told the Global Security Forum in Doha: 'When it comes to energy, we have not yet reached the peak,' warning of further supply and trade disruption in coming months, Al Jazeera reported.
sections.whyItMatters: One tanker through Suez does not reopen a route. It shows Qatar testing whether the Red Sea is passable at all — and it is doing so while its own government says the worst is still ahead.

sections.heading: Rubio's two-stop energy tour: Central Asia, then Jamnagar
sections.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio met the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan in Samarkand on October 19 under the C5+1 format, accompanied by a delegation of more than 100 US companies pursuing energy, critical minerals and infrastructure deals, per Oilprice and Uzbek media.

He arrives in Mumbai on Tuesday for a three-day India visit, meeting External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and travelling to Gujarat's Jamnagar refining hub on October 21, according to India's MEA schedule. A long-delayed US-India trade agreement is described as close to finalisation. Rubio said the US can help partners cope with the energy crisis — a pointed offer given India's continued Russian crude purchases, with New Delhi having already lifted Middle East imports to about 3 million b/d while cutting Russian flows to roughly 1.75 million b/d.

The critical minerals dimension matters more than the trade headline. Central Asia holds significant deposits, but processing capacity sits overwhelmingly with China, which is why Washington is pushing commercial deals rather than declarations.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is trying to convert an oil crisis into long-term supply access — Central Asian minerals and Indian refining scale — before China locks either down. The Jamnagar stop is where the pitch gets tested.

sections.heading: Beijing moves from solar exports to solar technology controls
sections.body:
China's solar equipment exports fell 6.4% year on year in September to 1.21 million metric tons of cells and panels, extending a 9.5% year-to-date decline, per customs data cited by Reuters. Exports have dropped since May, after Beijing scrapped the VAT export rebate on PV products effective April 1; a similar rebate on battery products ends January 1, 2027.

More consequential: the Commerce and Science ministries opened a one-month consultation on restricting or banning exports of up to 40 technologies across AI, biomedicine and solar — including perovskite, tandem, polysilicon, wafer and crystalline-silicon cell manufacturing processes.

The shift is from controlling goods to controlling the know-how to make them. Anyone planning a non-Chinese solar supply chain still needs those process technologies.
sections.whyItMatters: Export volume controls can be worked around with new factories. Process-technology controls cannot — they raise the cost of every alternative supply chain being built in the US, EU and India right now.

bottomLine: Today's moves point the same direction: the energy crisis is migrating from crude to products and routes. Gulf crude is recovering to about 80% of pre-war levels, but the Houthis are now threatening the Red Sea corridor that is Saudi Arabia's only Hormuz bypass, diesel remains 1.7 million b/d short with the IEA seeing no relief until 2027, and Washington is responding with an open-ended sanctions waiver, $8bn in farm fuel subsidies and talks with Europe on stockpile releases. Qatar's rare Suez LNG run and its own warning that the shock has not peaked suggest the gas side lags the oil recovery by months. Watch Mocha and the East-West pipeline restart — those two things, more than any OPEC meeting, set the price path into winter.
sources: Middle East Eye, Al Jazeera, Anadolu Agency, ZeroHedge, Oilprice.com, Bloomberg, Reuters, AAA, International Energy Agency, India Ministry of External Affairs, Indian Express, The Hindu BusinessLine, Latestly/Times of India, APA News, Discovery Alert, RBC Capital Markets, UBS, Sparta Commodities
